question: Under Minnesota's motorcycle operating rules, where may a passenger legally ride?
choice_a: Anywhere on the motorcycle the rider allows
choice_b: Only on a permanent, regular passenger's seat on the motorcycle or in an attached sidecar
choice_c: On the fuel tank in front of the operator
choice_d: Standing on the rear footrests only
explanation: A passenger may ride only on a permanent, regular passenger's seat on the motorcycle or in a sidecar attached to the vehicle, and must be able to reach the footrests on each side with both feet while seated.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.IV, 'Motorcycle Operating Rules'

question: Why does the manual say only experienced riders should attempt to carry passengers or large loads?
choice_a: Passengers are only allowed on motorcycles with sidecars
choice_b: It is illegal for new riders to carry any cargo in Minnesota
choice_c: The extra weight affects how the motorcycle handles, requiring extra practice, preparation, and caution
choice_d: Extra weight has no effect on handling
explanation: The extra weight of a passenger or cargo will affect the way your motorcycle handles, requiring extra practice, preparation and caution. For this reason, only experienced riders should attempt to carry passengers or large loads.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.31, 'Carrying Passengers and Cargo'

question: What personal protective gear should a passenger wear?
choice_b: No gear is necessary for passengers
choice_c: Only a helmet, regardless of age
choice_d: The same level of personal protective gear as the operator
explanation: Be sure your passenger is properly attired, wearing the same level of personal protective gear as you, and that the motorcycle is equipped with passenger footrests.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.32, 'Equipment for Carrying a Passenger'

question: Where should a child passenger be seated on a motorcycle?
choice_a: Immediately behind the rider, never in front
choice_b: In front of the rider so they can be monitored
choice_d: In a sidecar only, never on the main seat
explanation: Children should be placed immediately behind the rider. A child sitting in front of the rider will not be able to properly balance and may interfere with the rider's control of the motorcycle.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.32, 'Preparing Your Passenger to Ride'

question: When a passenger is mounting the motorcycle, what should the operator do?
choice_a: Keep the transmission in first gear so the bike can move immediately
choice_b: Start the engine, put the transmission in neutral, and keep both feet on the ground with the front brake applied
choice_c: Turn off the engine until the passenger is fully seated
choice_d: Rev the engine to warm it up while the passenger mounts
explanation: A passenger should get on the motorcycle only after the rider has started the engine and put the transmission in neutral; as the passenger mounts, the rider should keep both feet on the ground and the front brake applied.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.32-33, 'Preparing Your Passenger to Ride'

question: What should a passenger be told to do through turns and curves?
choice_a: Sit upright and never lean at all
choice_b: Lean opposite the direction of the rider for balance
choice_c: Stay directly behind the rider and lean with the rider through the turn
choice_d: Shift their weight to the outside of the turn
explanation: A passenger should stay directly behind the rider and lean with the rider through turns and curves; it is helpful for the passenger to look over the rider's shoulder in the direction of the turn.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.32, 'Equipment for Carrying a Passenger'

question: When riding with a passenger, how should a rider typically approach curves, corners, or bumps compared to riding solo?
choice_a: Avoid curves entirely whenever a passenger is aboard
choice_b: Ride at the same speed, since a passenger has no effect on ground clearance
choice_c: Ride faster to compensate for the added weight
choice_d: Ride a little slower, since scraping the ground at lean angle could cause a loss of steering control
explanation: When riding with passengers, ride a little slower, especially through curves, corners, or bumps -- if any part of the motorcycle scrapes the ground at lean angle, steering control can be lost.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.33, 'Riding With Passengers'

question: With a passenger aboard, how should a rider approach stops compared to riding solo?
choice_a: Start slowing earlier and maintain a larger space cushion when slowing or stopping
choice_b: Brake later than usual since the extra weight improves traction
choice_c: There is no difference in stopping technique with a passenger
choice_d: Rely on the passenger to apply their own braking
explanation: When riding with passengers, start slowing earlier as you approach a stop, and maintain a larger space cushion whenever slowing or stopping; also wait for larger gaps to cross, enter, or merge in traffic.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.34, 'Riding With Passengers'

question: Where should cargo loads generally be placed on the motorcycle to minimize handling problems?
choice_a: As far behind the rear axle as possible
choice_b: Over or in front of the rear axle, not behind it
choice_c: On the handlebars for easy access
choice_d: Placement makes no difference to handling
explanation: Try to place the load over, or in front of, the rear axle. Mounting loads behind the rear axle can affect how the motorcycle turns and brakes, and can also cause a wobble.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.34, 'Tips for Traveling with Passengers and Cargo'

question: Why does the manual advise against attaching a load high on the motorcycle?
choice_a: High-mounted loads are always more aerodynamic
choice_b: It has no effect on handling as long as it is tied down
choice_c: It raises the motorcycle's center of gravity and can upset its balance
choice_d: It is only a concern for sidecar motorcycles
explanation: Secure loads low, or put them in saddlebags. Attaching a load higher raises the motorcycle's center of gravity and can upset its balance.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.34, 'Tips for Traveling with Passengers and Cargo'

question: If using saddlebags, how should they be loaded?
choice_a: Only the left saddlebag should be used at highway speed
choice_b: As heavy as possible on one side to counteract the passenger's weight
choice_c: Weight distribution between saddlebags does not matter
choice_d: With about the same weight on each side, since an uneven load can pull the motorcycle to one side
explanation: If you use saddlebags, load each with about the same weight -- an uneven load can cause the motorcycle to pull to one side, and overloading may also cause the bags to catch in the wheel or chain.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.34, 'Tips for Traveling with Passengers and Cargo'

question: Why does the manual prefer elastic cords with more than one attachment point over rope for securing a load?
choice_a: A loose load or a rope that stretches or comes loose could catch in the wheel or chain and cause a skid
choice_b: Rope is illegal to use for securing motorcycle cargo
choice_c: Elastic cords are required by the manufacturer's warranty
choice_d: There is no real difference between rope and elastic cords
explanation: Fasten loads securely with elastic cords with more than one attachment point per side. Rope can stretch and knots can come loose, permitting the load to shift or fall or catch in the wheel or chain, causing it to lock up and skid.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.34, 'Tips for Traveling with Passengers and Cargo'

question: Before a fully loaded trip, what does the manual recommend doing with the motorcycle first?
choice_a: Skip any test ride, since loading doesn't affect handling
choice_b: Take a test ride through familiar neighborhood roads to check the loaded handling and confirm nothing scrapes or interferes with steering
choice_c: Only check the tire pressure and nothing else
choice_d: Have a passenger test-ride the motorcycle alone first
explanation: Prior to starting out, take a test ride with your fully loaded motorcycle through familiar neighborhood roads; be sure suspension settings are correct and that the side stand, footrests, and exhaust don't scrape, and that the tank bag doesn't restrict steering.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.34, 'Pre-Ride Test'

question: How does a full load and passenger typically affect a motorcycle's acceleration and stopping distance?
choice_a: A full load has no measurable effect on performance
choice_b: Acceleration and braking performance improve with a full load
choice_c: Acceleration is lower, increasing passing times and distances, and stopping distance may increase
choice_d: Only stopping distance is affected, never acceleration
explanation: The performance of a fully loaded motorcycle will differ from what you're used to -- power when accelerating will be lower, increasing passing times and distances, and stopping distances may increase as well.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.34-35, 'Pre-Ride Test'
